title: Why an upstream supply shock can set off a wave of euro-area repricing
summary: Mishel Ghassibe and Anton Nakov argue that the speed and breadth of post-pandemic euro area inflation are easier to explain when firms buy inputs from one another and choose when to reset prices. The two ingredients interact. An increase in the cost of a widely used input can make repricing worthwhile for many downstream producers at once. Their new prices become other firms’ costs, potentially setting off another round. The authors’ model reproduces both the surge in inflation towards 11% and the increase in the share of prices changing. This is a research result about transmission and model fit, offered in the authors’ own names. It carries no Governing Council guidance on the policy rate (pp. 1, 4–6).

Start with an individual firm. Revising a price requires effort, so a small difference between its current price and its preferred price may be tolerated. A larger difference is worth correcting. In models that give each firm a random chance to reprice at fixed probabilities, the aggregate frequency of price changes cannot respond in this way. But endogenous repricing alone leaves out the fact that most producers use intermediate inputs. If an energy supplier changes its price, even a firm with unchanged demand for its own product may suddenly find its existing price unattractive. The key variable for transmission is therefore the input’s place in the network, alongside the size of its price change (pp. 1–2).

The same links can damp an aggregate demand impulse. After a monetary or fiscal expansion, sales rise but firms’ input costs initially adjust only partially. Frictions at suppliers restrain the rise in intermediate prices, so the incentive for downstream producers to revise prices can remain modest. Some of the expansion then appears in real activity. A sufficiently large adverse productivity or input supply shock produces a different response: higher costs cross adjustment thresholds in many sectors, falling real output accompanies rising prices, and feedback through the network can raise costs again in the originating sector. A small disturbance at the same upstream point need not have a proportionately smaller version of the large disturbance’s effect. It can leave many firms below their repricing thresholds.

Chart 1 gives the distinction a concrete interpretation. It plots the modelled fraction of prices adjusting against the size of the shock, comparing the network economy with a version without input-output links. For demand shocks, repricing away from the centre is weaker in the network model. For aggregate productivity shocks, it increases much more sharply as shocks become large. The vertical axis is the frequency of adjustment, so more price changes can occur for shocks of either sign. A high point on either curve does not by itself establish the direction of inflation. Nor are these probabilities inferred directly from a particular month’s observed commodity move. They come from model experiments (p. 3).

The authors then represent almost 40 euro area sectors and feed in a combination of reopening demand, reduced labour supply and higher global food and energy prices after 2020. Chart 2 compares actual outcomes with three model variants. One holds the adjustment frequency constant by construction. Another lets firms determine when to reprice but omits production networks. The full model allows both mechanisms. The advantage the authors claim is its ability to describe the joint behaviour of inflation and repricing. The plotted model and data paths still diverge at particular dates and peaks. A better historical fit on two series does not establish that the network model identified each shock precisely or forecast the episode in real time (pp. 4–5).

For investors, the implication is that the breadth of inflation need not identify its origin. Many unrelated consumer prices can change because their producers face a common upstream constraint. A demand diagnosis based on breadth alone could therefore overstate the amount of demand destruction needed to suppress the initial impulse. Conversely, in this model monetary tightening can have a considerable effect on real output even when the immediate price response to a demand shock is muted. The authors favour monitoring important suppliers and firms’ repricing decisions alongside aggregates. They do not supply an operational threshold for an inflation warning, an optimal interest-rate response for the episode or a rule for converting a commodity shock into a trade (pp. 4–6).

questions.question: Would the mechanism have identified an inflation surge using information actually available beforehand?
questions.detail: The comparison in Chart 2 is fitted to the post-2020 episode and its shocks. Its value for policy-path risk depends on advance warning. Reconstruct publication vintages for input prices, supply indicators and sector weights, then test whether a signal would have preceded growth in the observed frequency of price adjustments. Start with the authors’ technical paper cited in the bulletin for the model inputs and estimation timetable.

questions.question: Which suppliers matter most for the inflation distribution at a given point in the cycle?
questions.detail: Energy is the motivating example, yet the mechanism depends on how widely an input is used and how near customer firms already are to repricing. Consult sectoral input-output tables, granular producer prices and firm-level price surveys. Compare industries facing similar cost changes with different upstream dependence. This could distinguish a concentrated shock with little broader pass-through from one likely to affect inflation-sensitive assets.

questions.question: Does the model discriminate between a supply cascade and other explanations for widespread repricing?
questions.detail: The full model fits two aggregate series better than the alternatives shown. The bulletin gives no independent test of the order in which individual suppliers and customers changed prices. Seek linked industry data on sales volumes, margins, input costs and the timing of repricing, conditional on common demand. That distinction matters because two episodes with the same headline inflation rate can imply different output costs of a policy response.
